title: Hypertension: Measure Correctly, Confirm, Risk-Stratify, Then Treat
bottomLine: Under the 2025 Hypertension Canada primary-care guideline, adult hypertension is BP at or above 130/80 mm Hg when measured with a validated device under optimal standardized conditions. Confirm with out-of-office assessment when appropriate, treat overall cardiovascular risk, start medication at guideline thresholds, and aim for systolic BP below 130 mm Hg when tolerated.
recognize: Hypertension is usually asymptomatic; symptoms suggesting neurologic, cardiac, aortic, renal or retinal injury belong on the hypertensive-emergency pathway rather than routine chronic hypertension management.
White-coat and masked hypertension are reasons to use home or ambulatory measurements.
differentiate: Diagnosis threshold and medication-initiation threshold are not identical: pharmacotherapy is recommended at BP at or above 140/90 mm Hg, or systolic BP 130–139 mm Hg when cardiovascular risk is high.
Secondary hypertension becomes more likely with abrupt/young onset, resistant disease, hypokalemia, episodic adrenergic symptoms, kidney disease, sleep apnea or medication/substance clues.
assessment: Repeat BP using standardized technique and correct cuff; assess orthostatic symptoms where relevant.
Review ASCVD risk, diabetes, CKD, smoking, alcohol, NSAIDs, stimulants/decongestants, hormones, corticosteroids and other contributors.
workup: Use out-of-office BP assessment to confirm diagnosis or identify white-coat/masked hypertension when feasible.
Perform routine cardiovascular-risk/end-organ testing recommended by current Canadian guidance and targeted secondary-cause testing when the presentation warrants it.
management: Recommend healthy lifestyle changes for all adults with hypertension.
Start pharmacotherapy at the current Canadian thresholds and often use low-dose combination treatment when medication is required, individualized to compelling indications and tolerance.
Target systolic BP below 130 mm Hg when treatment is well tolerated; avoid overtreatment in patients with symptomatic hypotension/orthostasis.
medicationSafety: ACE inhibitors/ARBs are contraindicated in pregnancy and require preconception review.
Monitor creatinine/eGFR and potassium after clinically meaningful RAAS-blocker or MRA initiation/titration.
Avoid routine ACE inhibitor plus ARB combination.
counselling: Teach correct home BP technique and explain why repeated standardized readings are more useful than one anxious office value.
Use non-stigmatizing sodium, activity, alcohol, smoking and weight counselling.
followUp: Reassess BP, adverse effects and relevant labs after medication changes, then adjust toward target without sacrificing function or safety.
examTrap: Using the old 140/90 threshold as the definition of hypertension—or treating one nonstandardized high reading as established chronic hypertension.
oneLinePearl: In Canada now: define at 130/80, confirm properly, and treat medication thresholds/risk separately.

title: Echocardiography: Translate Structure and Hemodynamics Into the Clinical Syndrome
bottomLine: An echocardiogram answers structural and hemodynamic questions; it does not replace the patient. Interpret EF, chamber size, wall motion, valve disease, diastolic indices, RV function, pericardial fluid and estimated pressures in the context of symptoms, loading conditions and study quality.
recognize: Reduced EF can support systolic dysfunction, but normal/preserved EF does not exclude HF.

Regional wall-motion abnormality can support ischemic injury; RV dilation/dysfunction can occur with PE or pulmonary hypertension; significant valve lesions require severity plus ventricular response.
differentiate: Estimated pulmonary pressure on echo is a screening/likelihood tool, not definitive invasive hemodynamics.
Pericardial effusion is not tamponade without hemodynamic physiology.
A technically limited study should not be over-interpreted as normal.
assessment: Define the clinical question before ordering: new murmur, HF, cardiomyopathy, embolic source, pericardial disease or pulmonary-pressure concern.
Compare symptoms, exam, ECG and prior imaging.
workup: Use transthoracic echo first for most structural questions; TEE, contrast, stress echo or CMR are reserved for questions where added detail changes care.
Repeat imaging when symptoms, treatment or expected disease progression justify it—not simply because time has passed.
management: Act on clinically meaningful findings: initiate/refine HF therapy, refer significant valve disease, investigate new wall-motion abnormality, or escalate RV/pericardial emergencies.
Use cardiology expertise when measurements are discordant or intervention decisions depend on nuanced severity assessment.
medicationSafety: Avoid making major medication decisions from one isolated echo metric without BP, renal, rhythm and symptom context.
redFlags: New major RV dysfunction with PE concern
counselling: Explain that EF is one part of heart function and that symptoms can be important even with a 'normal EF'.
followUp: Close the loop on cardiology/valve/HF referrals and repeat echo according to lesion/clinical change.
examTrap: Reassuring a dyspneic patient because EF is normal while ignoring diastolic/valvular/right-heart findings.
oneLinePearl: Echo shows structure and flow; diagnosis still requires clinical correlation.
sourceBasis: Canadian Cardiovascular Society heart-failure and valvular-heart-disease practice resources

title: Cardiac CT and MRI: Choose Advanced Imaging for a Specific Question
bottomLine: Cardiac CT and CMR are problem-solving tests, not routine upgrades from echocardiography. Choose the modality that answers the clinical question—coronary anatomy/calcium, structural anatomy, tissue characterization, myocarditis/infiltrative disease, cardiomyopathy or viability—and review contrast, renal, rhythm/device and radiation considerations first.
recognize: Coronary CT angiography can assess coronary anatomy in selected stable patients; noncontrast calcium scoring addresses risk rather than acute ischemia.
CMR provides detailed ventricular volumes/function and tissue characterization useful in myocarditis, infiltrative disease, cardiomyopathy and selected structural questions.
differentiate: Advanced imaging is not a substitute for emergency ACS/PE/aortic workup when the patient is unstable.
Calcium score and coronary CT angiography answer different questions.
assessment: Define the diagnostic question, pretest probability, ability to cooperate/breath-hold, rhythm, renal function, allergy/contrast history, pregnancy and implanted device status.
workup: Use CT or CMR when results will change diagnosis, prognosis or management and when simpler testing is insufficient.
Confirm MRI device compatibility/safety and gadolinium/iodinated contrast suitability per current local radiology policy.
management: Use results to guide cardiology referral, CAD prevention/revascularization assessment, cardiomyopathy/myocarditis treatment or structural planning.
Avoid serial advanced imaging without a new clinical question.
medicationSafety: Rate-control medication used for coronary CT requires BP/conduction/asthma context.
Contrast decisions depend on current renal function and agent-specific/local radiology guidance.
redFlags: Severe contrast reaction history requiring alternative planning
counselling: Explain why the more advanced-looking test is not always the right first test and what decision the chosen study is meant to change.
followUp: Ensure incidental/high-risk findings are closed-loop and avoid duplicate imaging across systems.
examTrap: Ordering cardiac MRI or coronary CT before defining the question—or using calcium scoring to evaluate active chest pain.
oneLinePearl: Advanced cardiac imaging should answer one specific management-relevant question.
sourceBasis: Canadian Cardiovascular Society cardiac imaging practice resources

title: Cardiovascular Prevention: Treat Absolute Risk Across Blood Pressure, Lipids, Diabetes and Tobacco
bottomLine: Cardiovascular prevention is cumulative risk reduction, not management of isolated numbers. Identify established ASCVD and high-risk conditions first, then address BP, lipids, diabetes/CKD, smoking, activity, nutrition, sleep, weight, medication access and social barriers using shared decision-making.
recognize: Established ASCVD is secondary prevention and carries higher absolute benefit from intensive risk reduction.
Diabetes, CKD, familial dyslipidemia, hypertension and smoking can materially increase risk even before a first event.
differentiate: Primary and secondary prevention use different treatment intensity/benefit assumptions.
Aspirin is not a universal primary-prevention vitamin and can cause major bleeding.
assessment: Assess smoking/vaping, BP, lipids, diabetes, CKD, family/pregnancy history, obesity, activity, diet, sleep apnea, mental health, medication access and social determinants.
workup: Use validated Canadian risk estimation when applicable and guideline-indicated lipid/glucose/renal testing.
Do not over-screen low-risk asymptomatic patients with ECG/stress tests solely for reassurance.
management: Use Hypertension Canada 2025 BP treatment, CCS lipid therapy, diabetes/cardiorenal protection and smoking-cessation strategies according to indication.
Promote physical activity, nutrition and weight care without stigma and address medication affordability/access barriers.
Use antiplatelet therapy only for a defined prevention indication after bleeding-risk review.
medicationSafety: Avoid routine aspirin in low-risk primary prevention.
Risk-reduction combinations require monitoring for BP, renal function, potassium, hypoglycemia and bleeding according to the therapies used.
redFlags: Severe uncontrolled hypertension with organ injury
counselling: Discuss absolute benefit and prioritize the highest-yield changes with the patient rather than overwhelming them with a long checklist.
followUp: Track risk-factor control, medication tolerance/adherence and whether referrals/resources were actually accessed.
examTrap: Focusing on a mildly abnormal LDL while ignoring smoking, severe hypertension and diabetes—or prescribing aspirin to every middle-aged adult.
oneLinePearl: Prevent cardiovascular events by lowering total risk, not by chasing one number.

title: After Myocardial Infarction: Close the Secondary-Prevention Gap
bottomLine: Post-MI care is an active treatment phase. Reconcile antiplatelet/lipid/BP/HF therapies, assess LV function and ischemic symptoms, refer to cardiac rehabilitation, address smoking/diabetes/mental health, and close every transition-of-care loop rather than assuming discharge medications will manage themselves.
recognize: Recurrent ischemia, HF, arrhythmia, bleeding and medication intolerance are early post-MI threats.
Cardiac rehabilitation improves recovery/risk-factor management yet remains underused.
differentiate: Secondary prevention is not the same as acute MI treatment; the outpatient goal is durable risk reduction plus complication surveillance.
Dual antiplatelet duration and other therapy depend on ACS/PCI/bleeding context rather than one universal schedule.
assessment: Review symptoms, BP/HR, medication list/adherence/coverage, bleeding, LV function, smoking, diabetes, renal function, depression/anxiety and return-to-work/driving needs.
workup: Review discharge angiography/PCI and LV imaging, pending labs and whether repeat echo or rhythm/ischemia evaluation is actually indicated.
management: Implement the CCS Secondary Prevention Pathway: evidence-based antiplatelet therapy when indicated, intensive lipid lowering, BP/diabetes/HF therapy, smoking cessation and cardiac rehabilitation.
Refer recurrent angina, HF, significant arrhythmia or incomplete revascularization issues back to cardiology urgently as appropriate.
medicationSafety: Review bleeding with antiplatelet/anticoagulant combinations and avoid NSAIDs when possible because of CV/GI/renal risk.
Monitor renal function/potassium/BP with relevant HF/RAAS medications.
counselling: Reinforce that rehabilitation and medication adherence are part of treatment, not optional extras after the 'real' event is over.
followUp: Use early post-discharge follow-up and confirm rehab/cardiology/lab referrals were completed; adjust secondary-prevention targets over time.
examTrap: Refilling discharge medications indefinitely without checking bleeding, LV function, rehab referral, recurrent symptoms or whether guideline secondary-prevention goals are being met.
oneLinePearl: The weeks after MI are a treatment window, not a waiting room.
sourceBasis: Canadian Cardiovascular Society Secondary Prevention Pathway (2025; updated provider tools 2026)

title: Heart Failure Medication Titration: Start the Foundation, Monitor the Physiology
bottomLine: HFrEF medication optimization prioritizes early use of the four foundational disease-modifying classes as tolerated rather than maximizing one before adding the next. Titration is a repeated clinical cycle of congestion/perfusion, BP, heart rate, renal function, potassium and symptom review.
recognize: Foundational HFrEF therapy includes ARNI/RAAS inhibition, evidence-based beta blocker, MRA and SGLT2 inhibitor for suitable patients.
Diuretics improve congestion but are not a substitute for disease-modifying therapy.
differentiate: A small expected creatinine change after RAAS therapy is different from progressive AKI with hypotension/hyperkalemia.
Beta blockers should not be newly/aggressively titrated in cardiogenic shock or severe unstable decompensation.
assessment: At each titration review assess BP/orthostasis, HR/rhythm, volume status, weight/symptoms, renal function/electrolytes, adherence, interactions and affordability.
workup: Check creatinine/eGFR and potassium after clinically meaningful RAAS/ARNI/MRA changes; other monitoring is therapy/context specific.
Use repeat EF only when timing/result will influence device or other treatment decisions.
management: Introduce foundational classes at tolerated doses and uptitrate with close follow-up rather than waiting months to maximize one class.
Adjust diuretic to volume status and treat iron deficiency/AF/ischemia/HTN and other contributors.
Use current 2025 HFnrEF guidance for EF >40% rather than copying the HFrEF algorithm indiscriminately.
medicationSafety: Watch hyperkalemia, AKI and hypotension with RAAS/ARNI/MRA combinations.
SGLT2 inhibitors require sick-day/perioperative advice and euglycemic-DKA awareness.
NSAIDs can worsen fluid retention and renal function.
counselling: Teach why several lower-dose medicines may provide more disease-modifying benefit than one maximized drug and why lab follow-up matters.
followUp: Schedule follow-up after each meaningful change until foundational therapy and congestion are stable; reassess access/adherence at every step.
examTrap: Waiting to maximize one HFrEF drug before starting the other foundational classes—or titrating beta blocker during shock.
oneLinePearl: HF optimization is foundation first, then physiology-guided titration.
sourceBasis: Canadian Cardiovascular Society/Canadian Heart Failure Society HFrEF resources

title: Pacemakers and ICDs: Treat Bradycardia and Sudden-Death Risk for the Right Indication
bottomLine: Pacemakers and ICDs solve different problems. Pacemakers treat clinically important bradycardia/conduction disease; ICDs prevent sudden cardiac death in selected survivors/high-risk cardiomyopathy patients. Device candidacy requires documented rhythm/ventricular-risk context and optimized reversible/medical therapy—not a low heart rate or EF number in isolation.
recognize: Symptomatic sinus-node dysfunction and high-grade AV block are common pacing indications; transient/reversible bradycardia may not need permanent pacing.
ICD indications include selected secondary-prevention survivors and primary-prevention cardiomyopathy patients after appropriate therapy/risk assessment.
differentiate: A pacemaker does not terminate ventricular fibrillation unless it is part of a defibrillator system; an ICD is not implanted simply for asymptomatic sinus bradycardia.
EF thresholds/timing differ by disease/ischemic history and require current cardiology guidance after optimized therapy.
assessment: Assess symptoms/rhythm correlation, reversible causes/medications, QRS/conduction, ventricular function, ischemic history, arrhythmias, functional status, infection risk and goals of care.
workup: Use ECG/ambulatory monitoring and echocardiography plus ischemic/genetic evaluation when indicated; document optimization/waiting periods where guideline criteria require them.
management: Refer high-grade conduction disease/symptomatic bradycardia for pacing evaluation and qualifying sudden-death-risk patients for ICD assessment.
After implantation, arrange device-clinic/remote follow-up, wound monitoring and underlying HF/arrhythmia management.
medicationSafety: Review rate-slowing/antiarrhythmic drugs before attributing bradycardia to intrinsic disease.
Device implantation does not eliminate antiarrhythmic/HF or anticoagulation indications.
counselling: Discuss shock plan, driving/activity restrictions and device follow-up using current Canadian/provincial guidance.
followUp: Ensure device interrogation, HF/rhythm treatment and wound/lead surveillance are closed-loop.
examTrap: Implanting an ICD solely because EF is low before adequate therapy/timing/risk assessment—or using a pacemaker for an asymptomatic reversible medication-induced bradycardia.
oneLinePearl: Pacemakers fix rate/conduction; ICDs mitigate sudden-death risk—both need the right indication.
sourceBasis: Canadian Cardiovascular Society/Canadian Heart Rhythm Society device and heart-failure resources

title: Endocarditis Prophylaxis: Reserve Antibiotics for the Highest-Risk Cardiac Groups
bottomLine: Routine dental antibiotic prophylaxis is not recommended for most heart disease. CDA's current position reserves prophylaxis before relevant gingival/periapical/oral-mucosal dental procedures for patients at greatest risk of an adverse outcome from infective endocarditis.
recognize: CDA high-risk groups include prosthetic cardiac valves, prosthetic material used for valve repair, previous infective endocarditis, cardiac transplant with valvular disease, and specified high-risk congenital heart disease situations.
For fully repaired congenital defects using prosthetic material/device, the CDA high-risk period is the first six months; residual defects adjacent to prosthetic material remain high risk.
differentiate: Routine prophylaxis is not required solely for mitral valve prolapse, rheumatic heart disease, bicuspid valve disease, calcified aortic stenosis, routine ASD/VSD or hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
Prophylaxis applies to specified dental procedures involving gingival manipulation, the periapical region or oral-mucosal perforation—not every dental event.
assessment: Verify the exact cardiac condition/procedure history and whether prosthetic material/residual defect/transplant-valve disease is present.
Review allergy, pregnancy, prior C. difficile/antibiotic reactions and current medications before prophylaxis.
workup: No routine blood testing is required simply to decide prophylaxis; clarify uncertain cardiac anatomy/history with cardiology/dental records rather than prescribing 'just in case'.
management: Give the current recommended single-dose dental prophylaxis regimen only when both the patient and dental procedure meet high-risk criteria.
Emphasize daily oral hygiene and routine dental care because everyday bacteremia burden matters.
If active infective endocarditis is suspected, prophylaxis is irrelevant—the patient needs blood cultures, echocardiographic evaluation and urgent treatment.
medicationSafety: Avoid unnecessary prophylaxis because allergic reactions, C. difficile and antimicrobial resistance can outweigh benefit.
Use current allergy-appropriate regimens rather than obsolete prophylactic choices.
redFlags: HF or neurologic complication suggesting active IE
counselling: Explain why many patients who once received antibiotics before dental work no longer need them and why oral hygiene remains important.
followUp: Document the exact qualifying cardiac condition so future dental decisions remain consistent and do not rely on vague 'heart murmur' labels.
examTrap: Prescribing dental prophylaxis for MVP, bicuspid aortic valve or hypertrophic cardiomyopathy without another high-risk condition.
oneLinePearl: Dental IE prophylaxis is for highest-risk cardiac outcomes, not every abnormal valve or murmur.
sourceBasis: Canadian Dental Association Position Statement: Prevention of Infective Endocarditis, revised February 2024
Heart & Stroke Foundation of Canada infective endocarditis patient guidance
